newsitem.title: USA: NYS monitor says NYC may face bigger outyear gaps.
newsitem.headline: NYS monitor says NYC may face bigger outyear gaps.

text.p: The New York State Financial Control Board sees a risk that New York City's big outyear budget gaps could widen even more, hitting over $4 billion in fiscal 2000 and 2001, a market source said Thursday.
The source, who declined to be named, cited a draft report by the oversight board, which was set up in 1975 to help resolve the city's financial crisis.
A board spokesman declined comment until the final report is released. "I refuse to comment on a draft that's subject to change."
The board's annual meeting is set for July 17.

New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, in his fiscal 1998 budget, estimated the gap in 2000 at almost $2.9 billion, and the one in 2001 at $2.7 billion. The state monitor board also saw the risk of a bigger gap in fiscal 1999--$2.8 billion, almost $800 million more than the mayor projected.

In the present fiscal year, which started July 1, the Financial Control Board identified $485 million of risks, the market source said. He noted, however, the board praised Giuliani for planning to make a downpayment on the fiscal 1999 gap by using $300 million of $500 million of 1998 reserves.

Like other monitors, it cautioned the city was relying on $2 billion of extra revenues, which mainly come from soaring profits on Wall Street. This camouflages the city's underlying failure to pull in enough revenue from resources that can be expected to come in every year, and leaves it vulnerable if the economy were to weaken.

While the Board of Education ended the 1997 fiscal year with about a $150 million surplus, which has left city officials wondering how much more spending it can manage, the state oversight board said New York City still faces risks in this area. Due to the rising number of pupils and costly special education programs, it said the Board of Education's budget has a structural gap of over $100 million a year.

The state board also faulted the city for not showing how it will pay for the rising cost of debt service, and recommended the full amount of capital maintenance programs be spent, to avoid costlier repairs later.

Finally, the market source said while New York City had cut its workforce and gained more control over overtime pay, wringing more savings out of entitlement programs would require the number of recipients to fall by an historic amount.
